newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish PM offers Gdansk shipyard plan, slams union.
newsitem.headline: Polish PM offers Gdansk shipyard plan, slams union.

text.p: Poland's Prime Minister held out a lifeline to save 2,000 jobs at the sinking Gdansk shipyard on Thursday, then accused the Solidarity union of fomenting chaos by illegal protests in the yard's defence.

"Don't try to build a second Albania in Poland," Premier Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz warned Solidarity in a speech to parliament, criticising union members who occupied three ministries in Warsaw on Wednesday and scuffled with police he had sent to expel them.

Solidarity this week launched nationwide protests against the government led by Cimoszewicz's ex-communists, demanding help for the shipyard where the union arose in 1980 to battle against communist rule, which was toppled in 1989.
The yard's plight is a symbolic rallying point for Solidarity Election Action (AWS), a right-leaning alliance the union has formed to fight elections due around September.
Cimoszewicz moved to take the wind from Solidarity's sails by proposing a rescue package for the yard, where the receiver this month began dismissing the last 3,800 workers.
He proposed that the successful Szczecin shipyard would set up, with the use of the Gdansk yard's assets, a new subsidiary to build ships for Poland's PZM merchant shipping company.
He said that under his plan the new company would build one ship for a German shipowner and complete another under construction, then build five vessels for PZM in 1998-2000.
"Such a plan allows employment of about 2,000 workers including about 1,100 in production at the outset," he said.

He said this was more likely to win credits from Polish banks which had refused finance for a contract to build five ships for the German owner, adding that the rest was now up to the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard's receiver.
Solidarity President Marian Krzaklewski said he had been urging Cimoszewicz for a year to do something for the yard.
"After a year of efforts at dialogue, I hope the proposal put by Premier Cimoszewicz is realistic," he told a news conference after a meeting with fellow union chiefs.

Cimoszewicz accused Solidarity, whose supporters have staged rowdy protests in Gdansk and Warsaw, of breaking the law by entering the ministries and starting clashes at one, in which policemen as well as several workers were injured.
"No matter how many times you burn me in effigy...I will not let you plunge Poland into anarchy," Cimoszewicz thundered.
He took full responsibility for sending in police and aimed a swipe at his grouping's Peasant Party coalition partners for distancing themselves from his decision.
Ex-President Lech Walesa, founder of Solidarity, said in Gdansk that the premier's speech was empty electioneering.
"These are the ramblings of a frustrated commie. He has started the election campaign already," Walesa told Reuters.
Krzaklewski said union chiefs had decided to call protests, but not strikes, at all workplaces in Poland on Tuesday.

He said the union, which held a several-thousand-strong march to Warsaw's parliament on Thursday, would repeat the action on Friday in the city and provincial capitals in protest against what it said was police violence against its members.
It was also considering a major demonstration in the capital on April 11, Krzaklewski added.
He ruled out a general strike, saying the union should focus on collecting for its fund to save the Gdansk yard.
"The best form of general strike is to vote in the coming elections for a non-communist programme," he said.
